01 / The whole system

How your
backtest works.

The program uses saved company data and prices to select stocks. It then checks how those stocks performed.

This guide explains each part, how the parts connect, and why some runs take longer. You do not need to read the code.

Saved dataOne set of selection rulesFour ways to use itNo downloads during a backtest

The main data flow

Save once. Prepare once.
Select many times.

A cache is saved data that the program can use again. Select a step to see its job.

1. The source data stays on your computer.

The raw folder holds the saved inputs. Ordinary preparation and backtests read these files. They do not contact the data supplier.

The browser and Python use the same selection rules. They use different prepared records for different dates.

02 / Four ways to use it

The date choice sets the path.

Latest picks and January backtests work in the saved HTML page. Custom dates and random dates need the local Python service.

Prepared in advance · Runs in the browser

A saved January-to-January test.

Prepared January records→Data inside the HTML→Browser selection→Results

The program buys stocks each January. It sells them at the next January date. The last book can cover part of a year.

Change the group, filters, metric or stock count in the browser. The page uses records already inside the HTML. It does not prepare new daily books.

Prepared in advance · Runs in the browser

A screen for the latest saved session.

Prepared latest records→Data inside the HTML→Browser selection→Stock list

Latest means the latest SPY session in the saved data. It does not mean a live market feed.

A company needs a price on that exact session. The saved company list must mark it as listed. Old stopped prices are excluded. These picks have no future holding return.

Prepared when needed · Uses the local Python service

A test on your chosen calendar.

Browser request→Local Python service→Saved or new dated books→Results in the browser

Choose the start date, end date and rebalance interval. Supported intervals are 1, 3, 6, 12 and 24 months.

Trade dates move forward to a saved SPY session. The end mark moves back to a session. A new buy/sell date pair usually needs a new book. A saved pair can be reused.

Many dated tests · Uses the local Python service

The same strategy on different trade dates.

Sample trade dates→Run each trial in order→Save each completed trial→Compare trial results

For each trial, the program selects one trading session from each frequency block. The last partial block also participates. Actual holding periods can have different lengths.

Trials use the same start and end window. Strategy and SPY hold cash until the first trade. More trials usually create more new date pairs and more work.

New runs use fresh dates by default. A seed is a number that lets you repeat the date choices. Use the same saved settings and seed to replay a batch.

What happens when you double-click start.cmd?

Windows starts Python. Python checks the data caches and the website build. It prepares stale files, starts the local service, then opens the browser. It opens a new port if the default port is in use.

03 / One holding period

From a report to a portfolio.

A book describes one buy date and one sell or mark date. The dated engine prepares the requested stock group before it applies your final filters.

  1. Choose a usable annual report.

    The report becomes available 90 days after its year-end. Availability must be before the buy date. A report older than 800 days is excluded.

  2. Prepare the requested stock group.

    The original group keeps the original 250-name screen. The broader group uses companies with saved prices. Only the requested group is prepared. Neither group covers the full market.

  3. Estimate values at the buy date.

    The program uses saved prices to update report market cap. It adds report net debt to estimate enterprise value. A missing buy price excludes a stock.

  4. Prepare metrics and holding returns.

    The program calculates both supported EBITDA metrics for the requested group. It uses dividend-adjusted prices for holding returns. It saves these records for the date pair.

  5. Filter, rank, then select.

    The program reads your chosen group. It applies your filters before ranking. Lower selected EV/EBITDA multiples rank first. It takes the ranks you request.

  6. Calculate the portfolio result.

    Each selected stock starts with the same weight. The program averages their holding returns. It joins the periods and compares the result with SPY.

Period return = sum of selected stock returns ÷ actual selected stock count
What if a stock stops trading?

The historical engine uses its last available price. The proceeds stay as cash until the next rebalance. A listed bankruptcy override gives a total loss. The override list is currently empty.

A later delisting does not change an earlier sale price. The original review covered 37 early stops. Additional stops in expanded or dated tests have not all received that review.

What if too few stocks pass the screen?

The program uses the stocks that pass. If 80 stocks pass a top-100 request, each starts with a weight of 1/80.

An empty holding period makes full-window strategy growth and CAGR unavailable. Random-date summaries keep incomplete trials visible. They exclude these trials from both paired distributions.

Which financial values are used?

The saved annual record includes market cap, enterprise value and EV/EBITDA. The program derives EBITDA and net debt from those values.

Estimated EV equals estimated market cap plus report net debt. The three-year metric uses mean EBITDA from three consecutive annual reports. Missing years exclude the stock from that metric.

The 90-day delay is an availability assumption. It is not proof of the actual filing date. Supplier data can include later revisions.

04 / Groups, filters and counts

Three choices. Three different jobs.

The stock group sets where to look. Filters set which stocks can pass. The stock count sets how many to take.

The stock group / Pool

Where should the program look?

Original candidate set: the original 250-name screen, with its report-size rules. Missing prices can reduce the usable count.

All stocks with cached prices: a broader saved-price group. It is still a partial market universe.

Filters and stock count

Which stocks, and how many?

Filters: market-cap bounds, minimum EV, selected metric yield, maximum multiple, sector and exchange.

Count: top 50, top 100, or a rank range. Top 100 does not expand the original 250-name screen.

Explore a setting change · Explanation only

Use the original candidate set. Apply your filters, rank the matching stocks, then take up to 50 stocks. Saved books for the same dates can be reused.

P/B below 1 is not a current filter.

The prepared data has no P/B field. First add suitable historical book values and prepared P/B values. Use values available at each buy date. A P/B filter would run before ranking. It must not use today’s P/B for past dates.

The controls above explain the architecture. They do not select real stocks or run a backtest.

05 / What gets reused

A new setting is not always a new book.

The dated engine saves each buy/sell date pair. It tracks completed stock groups separately. Your final filters and ranks use that group’s prepared records.

Current source · Requested-pool preparation
Your changeWhat the program does
Top 50 → Top 100Reuse the same dated books. Select a wider rank range.
Change an existing filterReuse the books. Filter and rank the saved records again.
Choose the other EBITDA metricReuse the books. Both supported metrics are already prepared.
Choose the other stock groupReuse that group if it is complete. Otherwise prepare its records for the same dates. Keep the first group’s records.
Use a new buy/sell date pairPrepare that book if it is not saved.
Run a new seedGenerate new trade dates. Prepare date pairs that are not saved.
Change source data or calculation codeRefresh the affected caches. Rebuild the saved website when needed.
↻

Replay can be fast because the work is already saved.

In the reference Windows test, 100 fresh trials took 467 seconds. A replay of those saved books took 5.7 seconds. These are different jobs.

What happens to books from the earlier engine?

The startup upgrade keeps saved prices and completed books when the research inputs are unchanged. Earlier books already contain both groups. The upgrade marks both as complete, including empty groups.

If other source inputs changed, the ordinary offline rebuild is still needed. The completion marker is saved with the group’s records. An interrupted write cannot mark a half-built group as complete.

What happens if I stop a run?

A fixed-date request saves its new books together. A random batch saves after each completed trial.

Unfinished writes roll back. Previously saved books remain. Restart the launcher and replay the saved settings and seed. Completed books can be reused. A stopped request does not resume by itself.

06 / Why new trials take time

Prepare the group
you actually request.

The earlier engine prepared both stock groups for every new date pair. The current source prepares only the requested group. Each group still gets both supported metrics and holding returns.

Earlier engine / Benchmark reference

New dates→Original groupBroader group→Select stocks

The earlier engine prepared the broader group for an original-group request. New trials created many extra records.

Requested-pool method / In current source

New dates→Requested group only→Select stocks

Prepare only the group you chose. A completion table tracks each group. Prepare the other group when needed. An empty group also counts as complete.

100 trials on native Windows Python

Measured test
Earlier engineBoth stock groups
7m 47s

Group + shared data4.4× faster · More memory
1m 46s

Test: original candidate set, top 50, annual random rebalances, 1996–2026. The end date was 20 October 2026. Seed: 20261022. Loading and per-trial saving are included. Common test-only cloning is excluded. The OS file cache was not cleared.

All selected holdings, prices, returns and exit statuses matched exactly. The measured gain applies to the original group. Selecting the broader group avoids much less work. Top 100 and P/B-filtered runs were not benchmarked.

Why fewer records help.
The reference test prepared 4,010,439 stock records. The requested-group test prepared 537,906. These are records across periods, not unique companies.

Why shared data is optional.
It added about 12.6 seconds of loading in the 100-trial test. At 24 trials, group-only took 32 seconds. The combined version took 35 seconds.

Source code and a running server can differ.

The requested-pool change is now in the source. These timings came from the benchmark prototypes, not a new test of that source version. Shared in-memory data remains a prototype. Relaunch start.cmd and use its new browser tab to load changed server code.

07 / Where each part lives

A map of the main parts.

Python handles preparation and dated backtests. JavaScript handles browser selection and display. SQLite stores data in local files.

PartIts job
Saved inputsraw/Holds company lists, annual metrics, stock prices, SPY prices and Treasury yields. Normal backtests read the saved data.
Research preparationscripts/research.py
data/research.sqlite		Prepares January and latest records. Checks the January baseline against the current reference report. Owns the shared SQL selection rules.
Financial rulesscripts/books.py
scripts/metrics.py		Choose reports, form stock groups, estimate values and calculate holding returns. Define the supported metrics and their formulas.
Dated backtestsscripts/schedules.py
data/schedules.sqlite		Stores daily prices. Sets trade calendars. Prepares the requested group and saves its completion marker. Uses the shared financial rules and SQL selector.

website/build.py

website/range.js

website/serve.py

Which report is the current reference?

Use results/summary-exits.txt. It keeps a stock at its last price when trading stops.

scripts/run.py still uses the older exit rule and writes to results/legacy/. Those files are not the current reference.

What do the charts and downloads show?

Browser downloads reflect the current selection. Baseline export files remain separate. Historical views show period returns and the growth of an equal-weight portfolio.

A stock’s contribution is its holding return divided by the actual stock count. Gain and loss pies are scaled separately. Their slices are not shares of net return.

The average random-trial CAGR is an average of trial results. It is not one portfolio return. Trial percentiles are not confidence intervals.

Which limits should I keep in mind?
  • The strategy uses equal starting weights and no commissions.
  • The saved-price group does not cover the full market.
  • Sector, exchange and listing status come from saved company metadata.
  • The 90-day report delay is an assumption. It is not a verified filing date.
  • Some supplier figures can include later revisions.
  • New early stops outside the original review can need further checks.

08 / Words used in this guide

The terms, without the code.

Cache
Saved data that the program can use again.
Book
The stock records for one buy date and one sell or mark date.
Pool / Stock group
The set of candidate stocks used for selection. It is separate from the final stock count.
Snapshot
A saved stock record for a particular date or holding period.
Filter
A condition that a stock must meet before ranking.
Rank
A stock’s position after filtering and sorting by the selected metric.
Rebalance
Select stocks again and give each selected stock the same starting weight.
Trial
One complete backtest with one set of sampled trade dates.
Seed / Date-set number
A number used to repeat random date choices with the same saved data and settings.
SQLite
A database engine that reads and writes local files. It does not need a separate database server.
Market cap
The estimated market value of the company’s equity.
EV / Enterprise value
In this model, estimated market cap plus report net debt.
EBITDA
Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. The model derives it from saved annual metrics.
EBITDA/EV and EV/EBITDA
Reciprocal ratios. A higher positive EBITDA/EV means a lower positive EV/EBITDA.
P/B
Price divided by book value. This filter is not available in the current prepared data.
CAGR
The constant annual growth rate that would produce the same total growth over the test window.
SPY
The S&P 500 ETF used for comparison. Its saved return series includes dividends.
API / Local service
The browser’s way to ask Python for a dated calculation. These requests use saved data on your computer.
